Greedy Uniformity on Trees:
Exact Obstruction and Near-Uniform Spiders **Abstract** Choose a uniformly random ordering of the vertices of a finite tree and run the usual greedy maximal-independent-set algorithm. We compare the resulting law on maximal independent sets with the uniform law. We prove that exact uniformity occurs only for the one-vertex tree and the single edge. The proof is structural: a diameter endpoint exposes a pendant star, and the remaining one-pendant-leaf case is resolved by a strict injection between exact permutation fibres obtained by swapping the pendant leaf with its support vertex. Exact uniformity is therefore rigid, but it can be approached closely. For an explicit mixed-spider family _Tk,l_ we count the maximal independent sets and compute the exact probability of every output. With _l_=2_k-k_ the total-variation bias is positive and satisfies \(b(T_{k,2^k-k})=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{4^k}\right)=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{logn_k}}{n_k^2}\right),n_k=2^k+k+1.\) The theorem package has also been formalised in Lean and registered with Palomar. These records document machine-checked formal verification and the checked axiom boundary; they are not peer review or a certificate of novelty. ## 1 Introduction A random ordering followed by a greedy scan is one of the simplest ways to construct a maximal independent set. Given a finite graph, scan the vertices in uniformly random order and accept a vertex exactly when none of its previously accepted neighbours has been accepted. The output is always a maximal independent set, but different maximal independent sets can have very different numbers of generating orders. The question studied here is when, for a tree, these permutation fibres happen to have equal size. Write M(_T_) for the maximal independent sets of a finite nonempty tree _T_, let G_T_ be the law of the greedy output, and let U_T_ be uniform on M(_T_). Our first result gives a complete obstruction to exact equality. **Theorem 1.1** (Exact obstruction)**.** _For every finite nonempty tree T,_ \(\mathsf{G}_T=\mathsf{U}_T\Longleftrightarrow T\cong K_1\text{\textit{or}}K_2.\) _Equivalently, if_ \(b(T)=d_\mathrm{TV}(\mathsf{G}_T,\mathsf{U}_T)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{I\in\mathcal{M}(T)}\left|\mathsf{G}_T(I)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}(T)|}\right|,\) _then b(T_)=0 _if and only if_ \(T\cong K_1\) _or K_2. The obstruction is qualitative, so it is natural to ask whether nontrivial connected trees can nevertheless have very small bias. They can. Let _Tk,l_ be the tree with a centre _c,k_ length-two arms _c-ui-vi_, and _l_ further leaves adjacent directly to _c_. John Fairfax-Ball October 1, 2026

<tbc>**Theorem 1.2** (Mixed spiders)**.** _Let_ \(k\ge 0\) _and_ \(l\ge 1\)_, and put N_=2_<sup>k</sup>. The tree T<sub>k,l</sub> has N_+1 _maximal independent sets. Its unique centre-containing maximal independent set has greedy probability_<tbc>

\(p_c=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=0}^k\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{j}\frac{1}{l+2j+1},\)

<tbc>_and each particular non-centre maximal independent set containing exactly j of the inner vertices u<sub>i</sub> has probability_

\(q_j=\frac{l+2j}{N(l+2j+1)},\)

_with multiplicity_ \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{j}\).

_For_ \(k\ge 1\)_, under the tuning l_=2_<sup>k</sup>-k, set A_=2_<sup>k</sup>_+1_, let J_∼Bin(_k,_1/2)_, and put W_=2_J-k. Then_

\(b(T_{k,2^k-k})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbb{E}\frac{W^2}{A^2(A+W)}+\mathbb{E}\frac{|W|}{A(A+W)}\right)>0.\)

_Consequently, with n<sub>k</sub>_=2_<sup>k</sup>+k_+1,

\(b(T_{k,2^k-k})=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{4^k}\right)=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{logn_k}}{n_k^2}\right)(k\rightarrow\infty).\)

Thus exact flatness of the greedy terminal law is confined to the two trivial trees, while an explicit connected sequence approaches the flat law with the upper bound \(O(\sqrt{logn}/n^2)\) along its vertex counts. We do not prove an all-_n_ upper bound, a matching lower bound, an extremal characterization, or optimality of the mixed-spider family.

The stochastic process itself is classical, as are random-priority and random-sequential- adsorption viewpoints. A targeted literature audit described in section 3 found no checked source containing either theorem 1.1 or the formulas and tuning in theorem 1.2; because such searches cannot certify worldwide priority, we use the deliberately bounded assessment that the contribution-level results are _plausibly new with bounded uncertainty_.

## 2 Model and permutation fibres

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be a finite simple graph and let \(\pi=(v_1,\dots,v_n)\) be an ordering of _V_ . Starting from the empty set, scan _v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>n</sub>_ and accept _v<sub>i</sub>_ if it has no accepted neighbour. Denote the output by \(\mathrm{Greedy}(G,\pi)\). Every rejected vertex has an accepted neighbour at the moment it is scanned, so the final set is independent and dominates every vertex outside it; hence it is maximal independent.

For \(I\in\mathcal{M}(G)\) define its _permutation fibre_<tbc>

\(\mathcal{F}_G(I)=\{\pi:\mathrm{Greedy}(G,\pi)=I\},g_G(I)=|\mathcal{F}_G(I)|.\)

<tbc>Since all |_V_|! orders are equally likely,

\(\mathsf{G}_G(I)=\frac{g_G(I)}{|V|!}.\)

Therefore G_<sub>G</sub>_ is uniform on M(_G_) exactly when _g<sub>G</sub>(I_) is constant over \(I\in\mathcal{M}(G)\).

We shall use a finite order certificate. Write \(u\prec_\pi v\) when _u_ appears before _v_ in \(\pi\).

**Lemma 2.1** (Order certificate)**.** _Let_ \(I\in\mathcal{M}(G)\)_. Then_ \(\mathrm{Greedy}(G,\pi)=I\) _if and only if every_ \(w\notin I\) _has a neighbour_ \(u\in I\) _with_ \(u\prec_\pi w\).

_Proof._ If the output is _I_, every \(w\notin I\) was rejected by a previously accepted neighbour, which necessarily belongs to _I_.

Conversely, assume the stated condition and suppose that some vertex outside _I_ is accepted. Choose the earliest accepted such vertex _w_. By hypothesis there is \(u\in I\cap N(w)\) with \(u\prec_\pi w\). If _u_ had been rejected, it would have had an earlier accepted neighbour. Since _I_ is independent, that neighbour would lie outside _I_, contradicting the choice of _w_. Thus _u_ was accepted before _w_, forcing _w_ to be rejected, a contradiction. Hence no outside vertex is accepted, and every vertex of _I_ is accepted because _I_ is independent.

For background and computation it is also useful to condition on the first scanned vertex. If \(I\in\mathcal{M}(G)\) and _n_=|_V(G_)|_\>_0, then

\(\mathsf{G}_G(I)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v\in I}\mathsf{G}_{G-N[v]}(I\backslash\{v\}),\) (1)

with the empty-graph probability interpreted as 1. The recurrence is elementary: the first vertex must lie in _I_, and after accepting _v_ only the relative order on _G-N_\[_v_\] remains relevant. We use (1) only as background and as a computational check, not in the shortest proof of theorem 1.1.

## 3 Related work and novelty boundary

Random-order greedy maximal independent sets have been studied in several forms. Krivelevich, Mészáros, Michaeli and Shikhelman study the same uniformly random vertex-order process and its equivalent continuous arrival-time formulation, with emphasis on output size, density and local limits \[6\]. Gazmuri’s random greedy deletion algorithm is another equivalent finite implementation; Dall’Asta, Pin and Ramezanpour discuss it in a statistical-mechanics treatment of maximal independent sets and explicitly distinguish a dynamical measure from a flat blocked- state ensemble \[2, 5\]. Blocking random sequential adsorption and parking models supply further background on greedy occupation processes on graphs and trees \[3, 9, 10, 12\].

For fixed deterministic graphs, the closest exact-uniformity source located in the final audit is Kryven, Versendaal and de Vries \[7\]. Their iterative maximal independent set process chooses uniformly from currently available vertices and is therefore equivalent in law, on a fixed finite graph, to restricting a uniformly random permutation as vertices are removed. Their Proposition 3.8 gives a _sufficient_ structural condition--regular independent sets--under which the terminal maximal independent set is uniform. The checked version does not state the converse. Their stronger 2-uniformity condition and its classification therefore do not classify all graphs with exactly uniform greedy output. On connected trees their sufficient regular-independent-set hypothesis already forces ordinary vertex regularity, leaving only the trivial tree cases, but that one-way implication does not prove the necessity direction of theorem 1.1.

Other nearby results concern different observables. Contat obtains an exact distributional identity for the _size_ of the greedy independent set on a uniform Cayley tree \[1\]. The RSA literature largely studies occupation probabilities and limiting densities rather than the complete terminal-set law. Gadouleau and Kutner study the same deterministic greedy MIS map from an ordering; in particular, their _P_<sub>3</sub> example displays unequal permutation fibres, but their main questions concern reachability and fixing orders rather than random-output equiprobability \[4\]. The maximal-independent-set counting inequality used below sits in standard counting territory; compare Sagan and Vatter’s _m_-bound \[11\].

These sources make several boundaries important. We make no novelty claim for the greedy process, its random-priority representation, random sequential adsorption, the dynamic-versus- flat comparison, first-choice recurrences, elementary fibre counting, maximal-independent-set counting bounds, or diameter-end geometry. The contribution-level claims are the exact tree obstruction in theorem 1.1 and the exact mixed-spider formulas and tuned near-uniform sequence<tbc>

in theorem 1.2. The literature search was broad but not exhaustive, so throughout we retain the assessment _plausibly new with bounded uncertainty_ rather than a priority claim.

## 4 The exact obstruction on trees

We first record a simple counting fact. Let _m(H_)=|M(_H_)|, with \(m(\varnothing)=1\).

**Lemma 4.1.** _For every finite graph H and vertex z,_

\(m(H)\le 2m(H-z).\)

_Proof._ Split M(_H_) according to whether _z_ is present. Maximal independent sets excluding _z_ are maximal in _H-z_, so there are at most _m(H-z_) of them. Those containing _z_, after deleting _z_, are in bijection with M(_H-N_\[_z_\]).

It remains to show \(m(H-N[z])\le m(H-z)\). For each \(J\in\mathcal{M}(H-N[z])\), choose a maximal independent extension \(\widehat{J}\) in _H-z_. This map is injective: maximality of _J_ in _H-N_\[_z_\] forces

\(\widehat{J}\cap V(H-N[z])=J.\)

Thus \(m(H-N[z])\le m(H-z)\) and the claim follows.

The tree geometry is equally elementary.

**Lemma 4.2** (Diameter-end structure)**.** _Let T have diameter at least_ 3 _and let_ \(v_0v_1\cdots v_d\) _be a diameter path. Put y=v_<sub>1</sub> _and z=v_<sub>2</sub>_. Every neighbour of y other than z is a leaf. Hence y has_ \(r\ge 1\) _leaf neighbours and exactly one nonleaf neighbour z._

_Proof._ The endpoint _v_<sub>0</sub> is a leaf. If a neighbour \(w\neq z\) of _y_ were nonleaf, the component beyond _w_ would contain a leaf _a_ with \(\mathrm{dist}(a,y)\ge 2\). The path from _a_ through _y,z,...,v<sub>d</sub>_ would then have length at least _d_+1, contradicting maximality of the diameter.

Let _L_ be the set of leaf neighbours of _y_, with _r_=|_L_|. Delete \(L\cup\{y\}\) and let _R_ be the remaining component containing _z_; put _F=R-z=T-N_\[_y_\]. The maximal independent sets containing _y_ are precisely<tbc>

\(\{y\}\cup A,A\in\mathcal{M}(F),\)

<tbc>so there are _m(F_). The maximal independent sets excluding _y_ must contain every leaf in _L_ and are precisely

\(L\cup B,B\in\mathcal{M}(R),\)

so there are _m(R_).

**Lemma 4.3** (Two or more pendant leaves)**.** _If_ \(r\ge 2\)_, then the greedy law on T is not uniform on_ M(_T)._

_Proof._ If _y_ is greedily selected, it must precede every leaf in _L_, since any earlier leaf is accepted immediately and blocks _y_. Hence

\(\mathbb{P}_\mathsf{G}(y\mathrm{selected})\le\frac{1}{r+1}.\)

When the nonleaf neighbour _z_ is present, the inequality is strict: among the orders in which _y_ is earliest in \(L\cup\{y\}\) are orders beginning _z,y_, but _z_ is then accepted first and blocks _y_.

Under the uniform law on maximal independent sets,<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}_\mathsf{U}(y\in I)=\frac{m(F)}{m(F)+m(R)}.\)

Applying theorem 4.1 to (_R,z_) gives \(m(R)\le 2m(F)\) and hence \(\mathbb{P}_\mathsf{U}(y\in I)\ge 1/3\). Therefore, if _z_ exists and \(r\ge 2\),

\(\mathbb{P}_\mathsf{G}(y\text{selected})<\frac{1}{r+1}\le\frac{1}{3}\le\mathbb{P}_\mathsf{U}(y\in I).\)

If there is no nonleaf neighbour, _T_ is a star with centre _y_. Its only maximal independent sets are {_y_} and _L_, so the uniform marginal of _y_ is 1/2, while the greedy marginal is 1/(_r_+1)_\<_1/2.

The remaining case is a support vertex with exactly one pendant leaf. This is where we compare exact permutation fibres.

**Lemma 4.4** (One pendant leaf)**.** _Assume the diameter is at least_ 3 _and r_=1_. Let x be the unique leaf neighbour of y, so locally x-y-z and_ deg(_y_)=2_. Then the greedy law on T is not uniform on_ M(_T)._

_Proof._ Let<tbc>

\(R=T-\{x,y\},F=R-z=T-N[y].\)

<tbc>Fix any \(A\in\mathcal{M}(F)\) and set \(I_y=\{y\}\cup A\). Define

\(I_x=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\{x\}\cup A, & \text{if}A\text{contains a neighbour of}z\text{in}R, \\
\{x,z\}\cup A, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{array}\right.\)

Both are maximal independent sets. Indeed, _I<sub>y</sub>_ is maximal because _A_ is maximal in _F_ and _y_ dominates _x_ and _z_. If _A_ dominates _z_, then _A_ is maximal in _R_, so \(\{x\}\cup A\) is maximal in _T_; if _A_ does not dominate _z_, then \(A\cup\{z\}\) is independent and maximal in _R_, so \(\{x,z\}\cup A\) is maximal in _T_.

Let \(\sigma\) be the transposition of the vertex labels _x_ and _y_, applied entrywise to an order. It is a bijection on all vertex orders. We compare fibres using theorem 2.1.

Suppose first that _A_ dominates _z_, so \(I_x=\{x\}\cup A\). For every \(\pi\in\mathcal{F}_T(I_x)\), the swapped order \(\sigma\pi\) lies in F_<sub>T</sub>(I<sub>y</sub>_). To see this, note first that in \(\pi\) the outside vertex _y_ can only be certified by its target neighbour _x_ among \(\{x\}\cup A\), so \(x\prec_\pi y\); after swapping, \(y\prec_{\sigma\pi} x\), certifying the outside leaf _x_ for target _I<sub>y</sub>_. The outside vertex _z_ is certified in \(\pi\) by some neighbour in _A_ because _x_ is not adjacent to _z_; that same witness remains earlier after the swap. Every other outside vertex lies in _F_\\_A_ and is certified by a vertex of _A_, all of which are fixed by \(\sigma\). Thus<tbc>

\(\sigma(\mathcal{F}_T(I_x))\subseteq\mathcal{F}_T(I_y).\)

<tbc>The inclusion is strict. Consider an order beginning _y,z_, then listing all vertices of _A_, then the remaining vertices. By theorem 2.1 it lies in F_<sub>T</sub>(I<sub>y</sub>_). Its swapped order begins _x,z_; both _x_ and _z_ are then accepted, so it cannot have output _I<sub>x</sub>_, which excludes _z_. Since \(\sigma\) is an involution,<tbc>

\(|\mathcal{F}_T(I_x)|<|\mathcal{F}_T(I_y)|.\)

<tbc>Now suppose that _A_ does not dominate _z_, so \(I_x=\{x,z\}\cup A\). The reverse inclusion holds:<tbc>

\(\sigma(\mathcal{F}_T(I_y))\subseteq\mathcal{F}_T(I_x).\)

<tbc>Indeed, for an order in the fibre of _I<sub>y</sub>_, the outside leaf _x_ is certified only by _y_, so after swapping the target vertex _x_ precedes and certifies the outside vertex _y_. Every vertex in _F_\\_A_ is certified by a fixed vertex of _A_, while _z_ is now itself in the target. Again the inclusion is strict. An order beginning _z,y_, then listing _x_, the vertices of _A_, and the remaining vertices belongs to F_<sub>T</sub>(I<sub>x</sub>_); after swapping it begins _z,x_, so _z_ is accepted although \(z\notin I_y\). Hence

\(|\mathcal{F}_T(I_y)|<|\mathcal{F}_T(I_x)|.\)

In either case two maximal independent sets have different fibre cardinalities, so their greedy probabilities differ.

_Proof of theorem 1.1._ For _K_<sub>1</sub> there is a single maximal independent set. For _K_<sub>2</sub> the first of the two vertices is accepted and blocks the other, so the two singleton maximal independent sets each have probability 1/2.

Now let \(|V(T)|\ge 3\). If _T_ has diameter 2, then it is a star with at least two leaves and theorem 4.3 applies. If the diameter is at least 3, use theorem 4.2. When the support vertex _y_ has at least two leaf neighbours, theorem 4.3 gives nonuniformity; when it has exactly one leaf neighbour, theorem 4.4 gives two maximal independent sets with unequal permutation-fibre sizes. Thus no tree on at least three vertices has uniform greedy terminal law.

## 5 Mixed spiders and exact output probabilities

Fix \(k\ge 0\) and \(l\ge 1\). The mixed spider _T<sub>k,l</sub>_ has centre _c_, length-two arms _c-u<sub>i</sub>-v<sub>i</sub>_ for \(1\le i\le k\), and direct leaves _w_<sub>1</sub>_,...,w<sub>l</sub>_ adjacent to _c_.

A maximal independent set containing _c_ is forced to contain every outer endpoint _v<sub>i</sub>_, and contains no _u<sub>i</sub>_ or direct leaf. Thus there is exactly one centre-containing maximal independent set. If _c_ is absent, every direct leaf must be present and each arm contributes exactly one of _u<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>i</sub>_. Hence there are 2_<sup>k</sup>_ non-centre maximal independent sets and

\(|\mathcal{M}(T_{k,l})|=2^k+1.\)

Put _N_=2_<sup>k</sup>_. Temporarily ignore _c_. On each arm the earlier of _u<sub>i</sub>_ and _v<sub>i</sub>_ is selected, and the relative orders on the _k_ disjoint pairs are equiprobable. Thus any prescribed arm pattern has probability 1_/N_.

Fix a non-centre pattern containing exactly _j_ inner vertices _u<sub>i</sub>_. Conditional on the required pair orientations, reinserting _c_ destroys that pattern precisely when _c_ is selected. This happens exactly when _c_ precedes every direct leaf and, on each of the _j_ inner-selected arms, precedes the corresponding _u<sub>i</sub>_. Under the conditioning \(u_i\prec v_i\), this is equivalent to _c_ being first among the _l_+2_j_+1 vertices consisting of _c_, all _l_ direct leaves, and both endpoints of those _j_ arms. Therefore<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}(c\text{is selected}|\text{prescribed arm pattern})=\frac{1}{l+2j+1}.\)

<tbc>It follows that each particular type-_j_ non-centre maximal independent set has probability<tbc>

\(q_j=\frac{1}{N}\left(1-\frac{1}{l+2j+1}\right)=\frac{l+2j}{N(l+2j+1)}.\) (2)

<tbc>There are \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{j}\) such patterns. Summing the complementary centre-selected contributions over all arm patterns gives

\(p_c=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=0}^k\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{j}\frac{1}{l+2j+1}.\) (3)

This proves the counting and exact-probability parts of theorem 1.2.

## 6 The tuned bias and its asymptotics

Now assume \(k\ge 1\). Set _N_=2_<sup>k</sup>_, choose

\(l=N-k,\)

and put _A=N_+1. Since \(k\ge 1\), the elementary inequality _k\<_2_<sup>k</sup>_ shows that _l\>_0. Let _J_∼Bin(_k,_1/2) and _W_=2_J-k_. The uniform mass on each maximal independent set is 1_/A_.

<tbc>For a type-_J_ non-centre output, (2) becomes<tbc>

\(q_J=\frac{N+W}{N(A+W)},\)

<tbc>and direct subtraction gives<tbc>

\(q_J-\frac{1}{A}=\frac{W}{NA(A+W)}.\) (4)

<tbc>Meanwhile, (3) is exactly<tbc>

\(p_c=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{A+W}.\)

<tbc>Since E_W_=0,

\(p_c-\frac{1}{A}=-\mathbb{E}\frac{W}{A(A+W)}\) (5)

\(=\mathbb{E}\frac{W^2}{A^2(A+W)}.\) (6)

The second identity follows by adding the zero term E(_W/A_<sup>2</sup>). Its right-hand side is positive because _A+W\>_0 and _W_ is nonzero with positive probability.

Using the multiplicities \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{j}\) to convert the non-centre sum to expectation under _J_, (4) and (6) yield the exact identity

\(b(T_{k,N-k})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbb{E}\frac{W^2}{A^2(A+W)}+\mathbb{E}\frac{|W|}{A(A+W)}\right)>0.\) (7)

This is the exact expectation identity in the frozen theorem package.

For the upper bound, \(W\ge-k\), so \(A+W\ge A-k\), while<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}W^2=k,\mathbb{E}|W|\le\sqrt{\mathbb{E}W^2}=\sqrt{k}.\)

<tbc>Consequently<tbc>

\(b(T_{k,N-k})\le\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{k}{A^2(A-k)}+\frac{\sqrt{k}}{A(A-k)}\right)=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{4^k}\right).\) (8)

<tbc>Finally, the vertex count is<tbc>

\(n_k=N+k+1.\)

<tbc>For \(k\ge 1\), \(N\le n_k\le 2N\), while _k_=log<sub>2</sub>_N=O_(log_n<sub>k</sub>_). Substituting these comparisons into (8) gives

\(b(T_{k,2^k-k})=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{logn_k}}{n_k^2}\right),\)

completing theorem 1.2.

## 7 Computational checks

Computation played a supporting role in theorem discovery and verification, but not in the all-tree proof. Exact rational arithmetic was used in two independent ways on small trees: direct enumeration of every vertex permutation, and the first-vertex recurrence (1). These methods agree on every nonisomorphic tree through seven vertices. A broader exact census generated all 436 nonisomorphic trees on one through eleven vertices (matching OEIS A000055 \[8\]); among them, exactly _K_<sub>1</sub> and _K_<sub>2</sub> have zero bias.

For the tuned mixed-spider family, some exact values are shown in table 1. These are checks of the closed formulas, not inputs to their proof.

<tbc>A targeted check of the structural proof was also run on all 434 nonisomorphic trees of orders three through eleven. In the one-pendant-leaf branch, 1103 paired maximal-independent-set comparisons had the strict fibre-probability direction predicted by theorem 4.4. These finite checks are corroborative only; section 4 is the proof for arbitrary finite trees.

## 9 Limitations and open directions

The results leave a natural extremal problem. Define

\(a_n=\mathrm{min}\{b(T):T\text{is a tree on}n\text{vertices}\}.\)

Theorem 1.1 says only that _a<sub>n</sub>\>_0 for every \(n\ge 3\), while Theorem 1.2 supplies a small-bias subsequence at the orders _n<sub>k</sub>_=2_<sup>k</sup>+k_+1. We do not determine _a<sub>n</sub>_, identify its minimisers, give a matching lower bound, or extend the mixed-spider estimate to every _n_. The small-order census in section 7 is not evidence for a general minimizer theorem.

It would also be interesting to classify exact uniformity beyond trees. Kryven-Versendaal-de Vries give a strong sufficient condition [7], but the general converse problem for the complete random-greedy terminal law is different. The permutation-fibre viewpoint used in theorem 4.4 suggests that local involutions and strict fibre embeddings may be useful in other sparse graph classes.
